# Prediction, Generation, and Optimization {#sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization}

![](images/ch05-cover-map.svg){fig-alt="Four architecture conditions map to direct comparison, prediction, generation, or optimization, with a named check, fallback, and stopping condition."}

::: {.epigraph}
> "Data can tell you that the people who took a medicine recovered faster than those who did not take it, but they can't tell you why."
>
> — Judea Pearl and Dana Mackenzie, *The Book of Why* (2018) [@PearlMackenzie2018BookOfWhy]
:::

Choosing a method for an architecture problem requires connecting the work to be done with the information available to do it. The data and representations developed in @sec-data-representations-world-models provide that starting point. Prediction estimates a candidate's consequences, generation constructs new candidates or revises existing designs, and optimization guides the search among alternatives. These methods can contribute separately or together, depending on the structure of the design space, available observations, and cost of evaluating candidates.

This chapter explains how to choose and combine methods by examining their assumptions, the data they need, and the evaluation effort they can save or introduce. Direct evaluation and conventional algorithms provide alternatives against which learned methods must earn their cost. Compiler tuning and cache evaluation illustrate how different candidate spaces and budgets lead to different choices. The aim is to identify an approach that can improve the architectural result, reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable result, or do both, while preserving the checks needed to establish those benefits. Connecting the chosen approach to real tools is the subject of @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces.

## Engineering Roles and Method Families

Building a design system requires separating the work it must perform from the methods available to perform it. Consider an illustrative design question within the Lighthouse vision pipeline: how should a small arithmetic datapath implement a required computation? We may need to construct an implementation, estimate its area and delay, and choose which alternative to evaluate next. Construction, estimation, and selection are engineering roles. A method supplies a way to perform one or more of those roles, using the available representation and returning an output that another component can use.

*Prediction* estimates a property or future state from the information supplied to it. For the datapath, a predictor might use its arithmetic structure, register locations, and target technology to estimate area or delay before detailed implementation. A learned predictor fits relationships from observations; an analytical model uses explicit relationships and assumptions. PowerNet provides a physical-design example: it estimates dynamic IR drop,[^fn-ir-drop-c05] the supply-voltage droop under switching current, from a design's power map before the signoff analysis runs [@XieEtAl2020PowerNet]. A prediction can help rank alternatives, but the estimate remains distinct from the observation used to check it.

*Generation* constructs a candidate artifact. For the datapath, a generator might construct a different arrangement of arithmetic operations and pipeline registers while preserving the required numerical behavior and satisfying the interface constraints. Its output is an implementation to check, rather than an estimate of an existing design. Construction may use templates, transformation rules, or a learned model. Language models have been used to draft electronic design automation (EDA) tool scripts [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA] and verification testbenches [@QiuEtAl2024AutoBench]. Generation can also propose a revised hardware organization or software implementation after feedback exposes a limitation. What it can change depends on the representation and constraints supplied to it; the resulting candidate must still be evaluated.

*Optimization* searches for alternatives that improve an objective while satisfying constraints. For the datapath, an optimizer might seek lower energy per operation subject to throughput, area, and timing limits. It chooses which implementation to evaluate next using the outcomes already available and the remaining evaluation budget. It may use predictions, direct measurements, or both to guide that choice. Examples include black-box search over accelerator configurations [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo] and learned policies for scheduling cluster resources [@MaoEtAl2016DeepRM]. Optimization therefore adds a selection strategy; it need not construct artifacts or predict their performance itself.

These distinctions let us describe a system more precisely than naming its model. A generator can propose datapaths, a predictor can estimate their area and delay, and an optimizer can choose which proposals warrant synthesis and implementation checks. Functional checks test whether the candidate preserves the required computation, while implementation analysis evaluates timing, area, and power under the specified conditions. The methods need compatible inputs and outputs, but they need not all be present. For a cache study with three specified capacities, direct evaluation may settle the comparison. An analytical roofline model[^fn-roofline-c05] may already expose the limiting resource in a larger study. Understanding what each method contributes is the basis for deciding which components the system needs.

::: {.callout-case-study title="A method family carries its assumptions"}
**The claim.** Itanium's explicitly parallel instruction computing (EPIC) design moved instruction scheduling out of hardware into the compiler, assuming explicit parallelism, predication, and speculation would allow wide execution with static scheduling [@SchlanskerRau2000EPIC].

**The gap.** Compilers had to resolve at *compile time* what dynamic hardware settles at *runtime*, including memory latencies and control flow revealed only during execution. General-purpose code lacked the assumed static parallelism.

**The lesson.** A method family commits to its assumptions as firmly as to its mechanism. A method is viable only when its required information is available at the moment of execution.
:::

Within each family, concrete techniques differ in the structure they use, the data they require, and the cost and reliability of their outputs. A regression model estimates relationships among supplied features, while a graph neural network (GNN) uses represented connectivity. A large language model (LLM) can generate code from supplied context, while a solver constructs solutions to encoded constraints. The family names the broad operation; the technique supplies its mechanism. Together with the engineering role and the system composition, these form four distinct questions about the design system (@tbl-role-by-stall-mode).

| **Decision layer** | **Question** | **Choices** | **Required discipline** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Engineering role** | What work must be done? | Propose, screen, search, critique, repair, check, explain, coordinate. | Name input, expected output, limits, and next check for each role. |
| **Method family** | What broad operation performs the role? | Prediction, generation, optimization, or domain-specific operations. | Select operations from required outputs and feedback rather than fixed pipelines. |
| **Technique** | What concrete mechanism fits the artifact and feedback? | Conventional, learned, or hybrid techniques (analytical models, regression, Gaussian processes, GNNs, LLMs, Bayesian optimizers, solvers, heuristics). | State assumptions, applicable conditions, costs, and failure modes. |
| **System composition** | Which components must work together? | Single technique plus tools, or composed generators, predictors, optimizers, and retrieval modules. | Assign every component distinct inputs, outputs, costs, and checks. |
: **A design system connects engineering jobs to computational mechanisms.** Four decision layers separate roles, method families, concrete techniques, and system compositions. {#tbl-role-by-stall-mode tbl-colwidths="[18,22,34,26]"}

The composition row matters when learned and conventional techniques work together. A neural code generator can propose a change, while a symbolic checker examines its syntax or types. Such combinations are often called neurosymbolic: learned components supply proposals or estimates, and symbolic components apply explicit rules. Compiler intermediate representations (IRs), abstract syntax trees (ASTs), and control-data flow graphs (CDFGs) provide structures on which those components can operate. Which properties are enforced depends on the actual rules and checks, not on the use of a hybrid label.

An agent can choose and invoke these components, but it still needs their inputs, permitted operations, and returned results to be defined. Assigning an agent to improve the datapath does not specify whether it should generate hardware code, fit a predictor, invoke a search algorithm, or call the synthesis tool directly. Foundation models and retrieval modules can support that work; they do not replace the distinctions among the methods the system uses.

Method families and operational layers answer different questions. An AI-driven optimizer tuning macro placement inside a fixed floorplan works within an established formulation (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration). An AI-native study may use generation to propose a different compute or memory organization and optimization to choose which alternative to evaluate next. Adding generation and prediction does not itself authorize interface changes, and exploration across interfaces does not require all three families. AI-native capability requires the workflow to carry coordinated generation and redesign through implementation and evaluation; permission to change an interface alone does not establish it. Method families describe how the workflow performs its engineering jobs (@fig-role-method-map).

![**Engineering tasks map dynamically across complementary method families.** Starting from declared engineering roles (proposing, screening, searching, critiquing, repairing, checking, explaining, or coordinating), direct tool evaluation provides the default baseline. When an added method is justified, selection routes through prediction, generation, or optimization, executed via conventional, learned, or hybrid mechanisms that terminate in inspectable outputs and property-specific checks.](images/fig-role-method-map){#fig-role-method-map width="100%" fig-alt="Four-stage map. Eight engineering roles connect through a many-to-many relationship to prediction, generation, optimization, and another method family, with a direct-tool option. The technique panel groups representative concrete mechanisms as conventional, learned, or hybrid. Every path ends with an inspectable output and a named next check."}

No engineering role binds uniquely to a single method family. Proposing does not mandate generation, screening does not mandate learned prediction, and searching does not mandate reinforcement learning. Inspectable outputs and property-specific checks govern every execution path.

Even within one family, a stronger benchmark score need not identify the best component for a workflow. In an automated repair loop, generation latency affects how quickly a candidate reaches its next compiler or simulator check. The software capability and inference-throughput comparison in @fig-agentic-sweet-spot illustrates two selection dimensions, but neither measures architecture-loop performance directly.

![**Model capability and inference throughput are separate selection dimensions.** Software problem-solving capability, measured by SWE-bench Verified pass rate [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench], is plotted against token generation throughput from Artificial Analysis provider benchmarks [@ArtificialAnalysis2026Briefcase]. The plotted regions suggest capability-throughput trade-offs for the sampled models; they do not establish an optimal model for architecture repair. End-to-end latency also depends on output length, retries, tool execution, and queueing.](images/plot_ch5.png){#fig-agentic-sweet-spot width="95%" fig-alt="Scatter plot showing SWE-bench Verified pass rate against token generation throughput for eight large language models, categorizing sweet spot, balanced trade-off, and throughput-bound regions."}

If generation dominates turnaround, faster output can make more repair attempts affordable. If simulation dominates, reducing generation time may save little, while a more capable model that reduces failed attempts could save expensive tool runs. We therefore need the cost of a completed, checked attempt before choosing between the plotted points. The capacity model below makes the downstream part of that comparison explicit.

## Anchoring Architectural Method Selection

The method families describe different computational capabilities. To use them in a design system, we need to connect those capabilities to the problem's structure and the information its tools can return. A learned predictor needs suitable observations, a generator needs a way to express permitted changes, and an optimizer needs an objective and feedback that distinguish useful alternatives. Method selection examines whether those requirements can be met and whether the resulting approach can improve the work within the available budget.

### Matching Methods to the Problem

Start with what can change. In the illustrative Lighthouse datapath, choosing among three supplied implementations is different from constructing a new arrangement of operations and registers. A small candidate set may permit direct evaluation. A larger space with explicit algebraic constraints may suit a solver or domain heuristic. Sequential choices, where one change affects the options available afterward, require a method that represents those dependencies. Known legality rules should constrain candidate construction or be checked before expensive evaluations.

Next ask what information will guide the method. A learned area predictor needs observations from relevant implementations and technology conditions. A generator needs the required computation and interface constraints, together with a representation in which it can express alternatives. An optimizer needs comparable feedback under a defined objective. Sparse observations do not rule out every method, but they can make fitting and checking a learned predictor more costly than using an analytical model or evaluating candidates directly. The data choices developed in @sec-data-representations-world-models therefore shape which techniques are practical.

These requirements connect the method's capability to the work it could improve. If candidates are difficult to construct, generation may help. If their evaluation is expensive, prediction may help screen them. If there are too many alternatives to test, optimization may help allocate the runs. @fig-method-selection-guide organizes these possibilities around the limiting work and keeps a credible conventional approach available for comparison.

![**Method selection compares added capability with a credible simpler path.** The initial question is whether an added method could improve the supported result or lower total cost. If so, bottlenecks in construction, evaluation cost, or search-space scale suggest generation, prediction, optimization, or composed pipelines worth comparing; saturated verification paths suggest throttling arrivals or expanding checking capacity. Every branch terminates at declared support bounds, total cost accounting, property-specific checks, fallbacks, and stopping rules.](images/fig-method-selection-guide){#fig-method-selection-guide width="100%" fig-alt="Conditional method-selection flow. An architecture decision and output lead to a test of whether an added method could improve the result or total cost. If not, retain the simpler conventional path. If so, limiting forms of work suggest methods worth comparing. Every branch ends at declared support, total cost, a named check, a fallback, and a stopping condition."}

The branches identify candidates for method selection, rather than sufficient reasons to adopt them. An expensive evaluator makes a cheap predictor attractive only if suitable data and useful accuracy can be obtained at an affordable cost. Likewise, a generator that drafts quickly may require enough repair and checking to erase that saving. A method comparison includes setup, data collection, training, qualification, inference, tool runtime, licenses, failed runs, and expert review.

Execution conditions can also determine which techniques are usable. Interactive repair may require short response times, while restrictions on proprietary register-transfer level (RTL) designs, foundry process design kits (PDKs), or licensed reports may require local execution. The consequences of an error matter as well. A suggestion that an engineer checks before use and an automated hardware edit entering a tool flow create different checking demands. Neither is made reliable simply by choosing a more capable model.

Finally, match the output to the check it needs. A compiler's syntax check cannot establish timing closure, and a predictor that ranks candidates does not establish that a finalist satisfies a power limit. A generated test can repeat the same misunderstanding as the generated design, so the checking path needs a way to expose shared errors. For each method, identify the conditions in which it can be used, the result its checks can establish, and what to do when those conditions fail. @tbl-method-role-limits collects these questions for a concrete study.

| **Attribute** | **Question to answer before selecting the approach** |
| --- | --- |
| **Job and question** | What work should the method improve: constructing candidates, estimating consequences, selecting evaluations, or checking a property? |
| **Inputs and support** | Which represented state, artifacts, observations, workloads, design regions, and process assumptions may be used? |
| **Approach status** | Is the method active, candidate, conditional, or disqualified for this problem? |
| **Output and legal actions** | What exact output will be produced, and which legal actions or mutations are permitted? |
| **Evaluator and checks** | Which evaluator, simulator, model, or tool checks the output, and what property-specific check qualifies it? |
| **Feedback cost** | What are the compute, sample collection, training, and license costs of this method? |
| **Support and failure mode** | Under which conditions is the method reliable, and how will invalid outputs or unreliable estimates be detected? |
| **Fallback** | What simpler method or deterministic tool will be used if this approach fails? |
| **Stopping rule** | When does search or generation terminate: resolved decision, spent budget, or rejected slate? |
: **Method choice connects computational requirements to the conditions of a study.** The questions summarize the intended job, required information, outputs, checks, costs, and limits before the evaluation budget is spent. {#tbl-method-role-limits tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Select the Smallest Sufficient Method"}
**The principle:** Select the simplest method (whether conventional analysis, heuristic search, learned prediction, or candidate generation) that relieves the identified bottleneck.

**The application:** Use a conventional tool as the comparator when it meets the evidence requirement. Add complexity only when the expected improvement in result quality or total cost warrants qualification, integration, and checking; retain the simpler path when the added method does not earn that cost.
:::

The remaining question is how much evaluation the chosen approach can request. A method may produce useful candidates faster than the available tools can check them. That mismatch makes downstream capacity part of method selection.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

### Quantifying Evaluation Capacity {#sec-sample-efficiency-under-expensive-feedback}

Producing a candidate creates work for the tools that evaluate it. A generator may draft a hardware implementation quickly, while simulation and physical implementation take much longer. An optimizer can create the same mismatch by requesting evaluations faster than the tools finish them (@sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search). To choose a useful proposal rate, we need to count both the evaluations each tool can complete and the fraction of candidates that reach it.

Evaluation paths often begin with cheaper checks that eliminate unsuitable candidates before more expensive work. Analytical rooflines test encoded bounds; Spike checks functional execution; gem5 models cycle-level contention. Implementation questions require other checks, such as static timing analysis (STA) in OpenSTA, power analysis under Unified Power Format (UPF) intent, and SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) checked with bounded model checking (BMC).[^fn-eda-signoff-c05] These tools establish different properties. The path must be chosen for the design question; a faster check cannot replace a slower one that establishes a different property.

The number of possible candidates can greatly exceed that path's capacity. Accelerator mapping and tensor-program search spaces studied with MAESTRO, AutoTVM, and Timeloop can span $10^6$ to $>10^{18}$ configurations [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO; @ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. Such spaces motivate pruning and selective evaluation. Even a small candidate set, however, can be costly if each evaluation is slow; candidate count and evaluation cost must be considered together.

Improving candidate quality can also increase the load. At an unchanged proposal rate, a generator whose outputs pass early checks more often sends more work to downstream tools. If those tools have spare capacity, they can evaluate more promising candidates. If they are already near capacity, the same improvement can produce a growing backlog. The relevant question is how the changed pass rates affect arrivals at each stage.

Model the path as a sequence of tool stages with a steady proposal rate $g$. For this calculation, assume fixed mean runtimes and conditional pass rates, separate capacity at each stage, and no retries or returning candidates.[^fn-feedback-c05] Stage $i$ has $c_i$ parallel slots and mean runtime $t_i$, giving a service capacity $\mu_i = c_i/t_i$. Its conditional pass rate $p_i$ is the fraction of its inputs that advance to the next stage.

Only candidates that pass all preceding stages reach stage $i$, so its offered arrival rate is $\lambda_i = g \prod_{j=1}^{i-1}p_j$. For the first stage, the product is one: every proposal arrives there. The ratio $\rho_i = \lambda_i/\mu_i$ compares incoming work with available service capacity. Keeping arrivals below capacity at every stage gives the load bound in @eq-queue-stability-bound [@Kleinrock1975QueueingSystems]:

$$
g < \min_i \left( \frac{\mu_i}{\prod_{j=1}^{i-1} p_j} \right).
$${#eq-queue-stability-bound}

The minimum identifies the stage that first runs out of capacity as proposals increase. This is a steady-flow model, not a prediction of turnaround time. Bursty arrivals and variable runtimes can cause waiting even below the bound, and a finite study may finish before a steady regime develops. Shared license pools and retries require additional accounting.

Consider the illustrative path in @tbl-candidate-check-capacity. At 32 proposals per day, a 1-minute structural screen advances one quarter of its inputs. Four simulation slots each take 8 hours per candidate and advance one tenth of their inputs. A single implementation slot takes 24 hours per candidate and advances half of its inputs. These are constructed parameters for the calculation, not measured runtimes for the Lighthouse datapath.

```{python}
#| echo: false
candidate_rate = 32.0
structural_capacity = 24.0 * 60.0
simulation_capacity = 4.0 * (24.0 / 8.0)
implementation_capacity = 1.0
structural_advance = 0.25
simulation_advance = 0.10
implementation_advance = 0.50

structural_load = candidate_rate / structural_capacity
simulation_arrival = candidate_rate * structural_advance
simulation_load = simulation_arrival / simulation_capacity
implementation_arrival = simulation_arrival * simulation_advance
implementation_load = implementation_arrival / implementation_capacity
finalist_rate = (
    candidate_rate
    * structural_advance
    * simulation_advance
    * implementation_advance
)
```

| **Tool stage before review** | **Parallel slots $c_i$** | **Mean time $t_i$** | **Capacity $\mu_i$** | **Conditional advance $p_i$** |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Structural and legality screen | 1 | 1 minute | 1,440/day | 0.25 |
| Cycle-level simulation | 4 | 8 hours | 12/day | 0.10 |
| Implementation screen | 1 | 24 hours | 1/day | 0.50 |
: **An illustrative pre-review tool-path capacity model exposes the active tool limit.** Values provide an inspectable load calculation rather than measurements of a specific commercial toolchain. {#tbl-candidate-check-capacity tbl-colwidths="[34,15,15,18,18]"}

We can now follow the workload through the table. Simulation receives $\lambda_2 = 32 \times 0.25 = 8\ \text{candidates/day}$. Its four slots provide $\mu_2 = 4 \times (24/8) = 12\ \text{candidates/day}$, giving $\rho_2 = 8/12 = 0.67$. Implementation receives $\lambda_3 = 8 \times 0.10 = 0.8\ \text{candidates/day}$ against a capacity of $1.0\ \text{candidate/day}$, giving $\rho_3 = 0.80$. The structural screen uses only 2.2% of its capacity ($32/1{,}440$). Implementation is closest to saturation and therefore limits further increases in the proposal rate.

Expected finalist throughput across an $M$-stage pipeline ($M=3$) is:

$$
q = g \prod_{i=1}^M p_i.
$${#eq-finalist-throughput}

Under these parameters, @eq-finalist-throughput yields 0.40 finalists per day. The final pass rate $p_3$ affects this output rate, but not the work entering the implementation stage: candidates consume that stage's service before they pass or fail. A finalist has cleared the modeled checks; choosing a design still requires comparison with the baseline and any further checks needed for the intended use.

Increasing proposals with the same pass rates raises each stage's load (@fig-candidate-check-capacity). At $g_{\text{max}} = 40\ \text{proposals/day}$, implementation reaches $\rho_3 = 1$; operation with spare capacity requires a rate below that boundary. Above it, sustained arrivals exceed service capacity. An unlimited queue would grow without bound, while a bounded execution system must delay, block, or reject submissions.

![**Downstream capacity limits the sustainable proposal rate.** Stage utilization $\rho_i = \lambda_i / \mu_i$ across the three stages in @tbl-candidate-check-capacity as proposal rate $g$ increases. Physical implementation ($\mu_3 = 1\ \text{candidate/day}$) reaches full utilization at $g_{\text{max}} = 40\ \text{proposals/day}$. The illustrated operating point of 32 proposals/day leaves this stage at 80% utilization. Sustained arrivals above the boundary exceed capacity; an unlimited queue would grow, while a bounded system must control submissions. Values are illustrative.](images/fig-candidate-check-capacity){#fig-candidate-check-capacity width="100%" fig-alt="Plot of candidate proposal rate g on the x-axis versus stage utilization rho_i on the y-axis across three verification stages. Structural screen (blue line) remains near zero, simulation (dashed orange line) climbs moderately, and physical implementation (solid red line) climbs rapidly, crossing the 100% queue stability threshold at g_max = 40 proposals per day. A callout box marks the selected operating point at g = 32 proposals per day and 80% utilization, while a red shaded region above g = 40 highlights the unstable queue backlog area."}

The bound applies to conventional optimizers and learned generators alike. If several agents produce candidates for the same tools, their combined arrival rate counts against the available capacity. Better early pass rates also require recalculating the bound: a larger fraction of the same proposal stream now reaches the expensive stages.

The execution harness can regulate submissions by limiting batch sizes or the number of outstanding evaluations. Token-bucket or leaky-bucket admission control provides other ways to enforce a rate limit. These controls act on candidate requests; a language model's token generation rate alone does not specify its demand for tool evaluations. Increasing filtering can reduce demand too, but only if the revised screen retains the candidates needed for the study's decision.

For method selection, this calculation identifies where additional capability could help. Faster proposals are useful when the evaluation path can absorb them. When it cannot, the study may need fewer proposals, more evaluation capacity, or a reliable cheaper screen. The last option raises a separate question: how much expensive work can screening actually save?

### Screening Cost and Validated Coverage

A cheap screen can reduce the work sent to an expensive evaluator, but running quickly is only part of its value. It must also resolve enough cases reliably. For the Lighthouse datapath, an early area estimate might reject an implementation that clearly exceeds the area limit. A candidate near the limit would still need a reference evaluation. The useful saving depends on how often the screen can make that decision within the study's allowed error, and on what it costs to check that the screening rule is reliable.

Selective classification studies the trade-off between the fraction of cases a model answers and its error on those answers; it permits the model to abstain on the remaining cases [@ElYanivWiener2010SelectiveClassification]. For architectural screening, *validated coverage* $f$ is the fraction of the target comparison stream that a qualified screening rule settles without the reference evaluation, under declared error limits. It is not simply the fraction of candidates rejected. A rule that rejects many useful designs may save tool time while defeating the purpose of the search.

To calculate the possible saving, count *service work*: the evaluation effort spent processing comparisons, excluding time waiting in queues. Let $c_{\mathrm{hi}}$ be the reference cost per comparison and $c_{\mathrm{cheap}}$ the cost of a cheap check, measured in the same units. This simplified model assigns a common reference cost to cases that are screened out and cases that proceed. If their costs differ systematically, the calculation must instead weight the work saved in each group.

Suppose a fraction $a$ of all comparisons receives a cheap check and a fraction $f \le a$ is settled there. The fraction $a-f$ pays for both checks, while the fraction $1-a$ goes directly to the reference path. Thus $1-f$ still incurs reference cost. Screening adds $a c_{\mathrm{cheap}}$ per original comparison, plus routing, qualification, auditing, and rework costs. Let $\epsilon \ge 0$ denote that additional overhead per comparison, normalized by $c_{\mathrm{hi}}$. Dividing the original reference cost by the resulting cost gives:

$$
S_{\mathrm{screen}} = \frac{1}{(1-f) + a \cdot (c_{\mathrm{cheap}}/c_{\mathrm{hi}}) + \epsilon} \le \frac{1}{(1-f) + f \cdot (c_{\mathrm{cheap}}/c_{\mathrm{hi}}) + \epsilon}.
$${#eq-screening-efficiency-bound}

For fixed coverage and costs, @eq-screening-efficiency-bound is largest when every cheap check settles its case ($a=f$). This is an ideal routing bound: in practice, the system may not know which cases will be settled until it runs the screen. Universal screening uses $a=1$ and pays the cheap-check cost on every comparison, including those that subsequently need the reference path.

Even if screening and its overhead become free, the remaining fraction $1-f$ still pays full reference cost. The speedup therefore approaches $1/(1-f)$, following the same unaffected-work argument as Amdahl's law [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. For fixed coverage below one, reducing screening cost cannot exceed this ceiling. The screen can also make the process more expensive if its cost and overhead exceed the reference work it avoids.

The earlier capacity example illustrates the distinction between rejection rate and validated coverage. Its structural screen forwards a quarter of its arrivals (@tbl-candidate-check-capacity). If the rejected fraction can legitimately bypass simulation under the required checks, it provides coverage of $0.75$ for that screening decision. Under the common-cost assumption, a free screen would then cap the reduction in simulation service work at $1/(1-0.75)$. The observed pass fraction alone does not establish that the rejected candidates were safe to discard.

The curves in @fig-rejection-bound-ceiling separate the effects of cost and coverage. At a given coverage, a cheaper screen produces a larger saving, and ideal routing avoids work that universal screening pays. All curves remain below the free-screen ceiling. At $f=0.6$, that ceiling is $2.5\times$; further gains require settling a larger fraction of comparisons reliably, not just executing the same screen faster.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-rejection-bound-ceiling
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Validated coverage sets the upper bound on screening speedup.** In the illustrative common-cost model of @eq-screening-efficiency-bound with zero overhead, evaluation service-work speedup (y-axis) is plotted against validated coverage $f$ (x-axis) across three cheap-to-reference cost ratios ($c_{\mathrm{cheap}}/c_{\mathrm{hi}} \in \{0.01, 0.1, 0.3\}$). Solid curves show ideal routing ($a=f$) and dashed curves show universal screening ($a=1$). Lowering check cost pushes performance toward the free-check ceiling $1/(1-f)$ (dashed black line); at $f=0.6$, speedup is capped at $2.5\times$ regardless of screening cost. Curves are constructed for illustration, not measured workflow speedups.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of evaluation service-work speedup against validated coverage f on the x-axis. A dashed ceiling curve traces one over one minus f, and three colored cost-ratio curves for 0.01, 0.1, and 0.3 sit below it; an annotated point marks f equals 0.6 capping the speedup at about 2.5x."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Constructed illustrative parameters: the cost ratios and coverage fractions below are
# author-chosen to show how the chapter's common-cost screening model behaves,
# not measured. Overhead is set to zero for the plotted curves.
f_grid = [0.95 * i / 399 for i in range(400)]
ratios = [
    {"label": "cost ratio 0.01", "r": 0.01, "color": COLORS["orange"]},
    {"label": "cost ratio 0.1", "r": 0.1, "color": COLORS["green"]},
    {"label": "cost ratio 0.3", "r": 0.3, "color": COLORS["red"]},
]

def s_review(cov, r, a):
    return 1.0 / ((1.0 - cov) + a * r)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.25, 3.0))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.86, top=0.82, bottom=0.16)

ceiling = [1.0 / (1.0 - x) for x in f_grid]
ax.fill_between(f_grid, ceiling, 30, color=COLORS["grid"], alpha=0.35, zorder=0)
ax.text(0.04, 9.0, "unreachable without more validated coverage", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["muted"], fontstyle="italic")
ax.plot(f_grid, ceiling, color=COLORS["ink"], linewidth=0.8, linestyle=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=2)

ax.axhline(1.0, color=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=0.7, zorder=1)
ax.text(0.93, 1.04, "no speedup", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["muted"])

for c in ratios:
    ax.plot(f_grid, [s_review(x, c["r"], x) for x in f_grid], color=c["color"], linewidth=1.9, zorder=3, label=c["label"])
    ax.plot(f_grid, [s_review(x, c["r"], 1.0) for x in f_grid], color=c["color"], linewidth=1.2, linestyle=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=3)

ax.scatter([0.6], [2.5], marker="o", s=22, facecolor=COLORS["note_fill"], edgecolor=COLORS["ink"], linewidth=1.3, zorder=4)
ax.text(0.58, 2.95, "f = 0.6 caps the speedup at 2.5x", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["ink"])

ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0, 0.95)
ax.set_ylim(0.7, 30)
ax.set_xlabel("validated coverage f  (share of cases settled without escalation)", fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylabel("evaluation service-work speedup", fontsize=7)
ax.set_xticks([0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8])
ax.set_yticks([1, 2, 5, 10, 20])
ax.set_yticklabels(["1x", "2x", "5x", "10x", "20x"], fontsize=6.4)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2, labelsize=6.4)
ax.grid(axis="both", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.5, zorder=0)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

legend = ax.legend(
    loc="lower left",
    bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 1.02),
    fontsize=6.0,
    frameon=True,
    facecolor="white",
    edgecolor="white",
    framealpha=0.92,
    handlelength=1.6,
    borderpad=0.15,
    labelspacing=0.3,
    ncol=1,
)
for text in legend.get_texts():
    text.set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

To use the bound in a study, estimate coverage and screening error on a representative sample of the whole target stream. Checking only the cases the screen chose to settle leaves performance on the omitted cases unknown and can introduce selection bias [@Heckman1979SampleSelectionBias]. Report the sampling procedure, uncertainty in the coverage estimate, and errors that matter to the decision, especially rejection of useful candidates. Shared assumptions between the screen and reference can hide errors from both; agreement establishes only what that reference path can check.

The capacity and screening models answer different questions. The first identifies how much candidate traffic each stage can serve. The second estimates the evaluation work a screen can avoid. A reduction in service work does not directly establish a reduction in elapsed time: queueing, parallel resources, and any costs omitted from the accounting still matter. Coverage must also be checked when the candidate population or hardware and software conditions change (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack). For a learned screen, the next issue is what its predictor can estimate and under which conditions those estimates are useful.

## Predictive Surrogates and Reference Paths {#sec-prediction-estimating-behavior-before-full-evaluation}

A predictive surrogate estimates a quantity that would otherwise require a more expensive evaluation. For the Lighthouse datapath, the quantity might be area or critical-path delay under a specified implementation flow. The surrogate receives a representation of a candidate and its relevant conditions, then returns an estimate. That estimate can help select candidates for evaluation, allowing a study to examine a larger space with fewer detailed tool runs [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling]. The useful question is whether the estimates preserve the distinctions the design decision depends on.

Building a learned surrogate starts with paired inputs and reference observations. A datapath area model might use operation counts, bit widths, register counts, and target-library information as inputs, with area reports from a specified synthesis flow as training targets. Fitting adjusts the model to those observations; evaluation on separate examples tests how well it predicts candidates it has not fitted. At use time, the input features must be available before the expensive run. Supplying a result extracted from that same run would defeat the intended saving. The representation choices in @sec-data-representations-world-models therefore determine both what the predictor can use and when it can be used.

The techniques differ in how they connect inputs to outputs. An analytical model calculates from explicit engineering relationships. Linear regression fits a weighted combination of supplied features; interaction features can represent effects that a simple sum would miss. Trees divide the feature space through successive tests, allowing different predictions in different regions. A Gaussian process uses a specified similarity function to relate observations and returns a predictive distribution; its uncertainty depends on those modeling assumptions. Neural networks learn nonlinear transformations, with sequence models exploiting ordered context and graph models exploiting represented connectivity. A hybrid can retain an analytical estimate and learn a correction to its repeatable error.

These are alternatives with different requirements, rather than a progression toward a universally better predictor. An inspectable model may suffice when a few known relationships control the metric. More flexible models become useful when the data captures interactions that simpler models miss. @tbl-prediction-techniques summarizes the structures each approach can use and the conditions that can make it unsuitable.

| **Predictive technique** | **Strong fit** | **Main reason to reject it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical / mechanistic cost model | Known relationships, limited data, inspectable assumptions. | Omitted interactions control the decision. |
| Linear / regularized regression | Stable tabular features, modest complexity. | Sharp response changes or uncaptured feature structure. |
| Decision trees / boosted forests | Tabular parameters, nonlinear interactions, mixed types. | Extrapolation into unobserved design regions. |
| Gaussian process | Costly evaluations, moderate dimensions, uncertainty coupling. | High dimensionality or dataset size making surrogate costly. |
| Neural network | Large datasets from matching conditions, complex nonlinearities. | Insufficient data coverage, latency limits, or confidentiality. |
| Sequence / transformer model | Programs, traces, reports, ordered context. | Token/sequence dataset size or deployment budget mismatch. |
| Graph neural network | Netlists, dependency graphs, circuit connectivity. | Node/edge features omit properties controlling the metric. |
| Analytical model + learned correction | Analytical model exists with repeatable residual error. | Correction data mismatch with current tool or workload. |
| Transition / world model | Actions alter subsequent states across multi-step planning. | Static scoring or direct tool feedback suffices. |
: **Predictive techniques differ in the structure and support they require.** Selection follows target consequences, data representations, available sample counts, and evaluation costs. {#tbl-prediction-techniques tbl-colwidths="[26,34,40]"}

The graph and sequence rows illustrate why model structure matters. Two datapaths can contain similar numbers of operations while connecting them into different paths. A graph model can use those dependencies rather than relying only on counts. At gate level, each net connects a driver to its load pins, which can be represented as a directed hypergraph. Connectivity and cell attributes provide useful information, but routing congestion and wire parasitics also depend on placement and physical context. A graph representation alone does not supply those missing conditions.

Ordered activity presents a different problem. A sequence model can use time-ordered waveform activity to distinguish events that aggregate toggle counts combine. Estimates of transient supply-voltage droop, dynamic power peaks, or glitch power also require the relevant timing and power-delivery information. Choosing a model that uses sequences cannot compensate for omitting the conditions that determine the requested quantity.

The final table row changes what is predicted. A static cost model scores a candidate in its present form. A transition model estimates how a represented state changes after an action. This becomes useful when a study must reason about a sequence of edits whose consequences depend on earlier choices.

> **Architecture world model.** A learned predictor of how represented design state, permitted actions, and operating conditions affect subsequent state or measured behavior [@HaSchmidhuber2018WorldModels]. When it is scoped to how state or decision-relevant consequences change after an action sequence under stated conditions, it is a transition model. Either way it is a predictive technique rather than a universal design theory.

Sequential macro placement illustrates a possible use. Placing a static random-access memory (SRAM) macro changes the occupied area and can affect routing access and the feasibility of later placements. A learned transition model would take the partial floorplan and a proposed placement action as inputs and estimate the resulting state, $\hat{s}' = \hat{T}(s,a)$. Applying the model repeatedly produces a rollout: a predicted sequence of states under proposed actions. This applies the model-based planning idea of @HaSchmidhuber2018WorldModels and @JannerEtAl2019MBPO to an architectural setting; it is not a claim that those studies established a qualified floorplanning model.

In such a composition, a planner could compare short predicted sequences, send a selected action to the placement tools, and replan using the returned state. Deterministic checks would still enforce encoded constraints such as nonoverlap. The transition model would need observations of state changes, rather than only scores for completed designs. Its value depends on whether the rollouts save enough tool work to offset fitting cost and accumulated prediction error. When direct feedback is cheap or only the current candidate's score matters, a static predictor or direct tool call may suffice.

Whether the predictor estimates a metric or a state transition, its output needs a reference against which error can be assessed. For the datapath, predicted area can be compared with the area returned by the specified implementation flow. Functional correctness requires its own check. Keeping the prediction and reference result separate allows us to measure the discrepancy and decide whether the model remains useful (@fig-architecture-cost-model).

![**Predictions and reference-tool observations remain distinct.** A represented state and proposed action can be evaluated through a predictive model and through the tools chosen for the target property. Paired estimates and observations allow prediction error to be assessed under identified conditions. The reference may itself be a simulation or analytical model; its output establishes only the properties that configured path can evaluate.](images/fig-architecture-cost-model){#fig-architecture-cost-model width="100%" fig-alt="A represented state and proposed action feed a scoped consequence model and a separate tool path. The prediction and tool observation remain distinct and both enter a versioned study record."}

During model qualification, both paths evaluate selected candidates so their outputs can be compared. During search, the surrogate may screen many candidates while only a subset reaches the reference tools. The selection rule and periodic checks determine whether that saving preserves the comparisons the study needs. Running both paths for every candidate would retain the reference cost the surrogate was intended to avoid.

The reference must match the quantity being predicted. A surrogate trained against microarchitectural simulation learns to approximate that simulator's observations, not every property of the eventual circuit. @fig-eval-fidelity-latency distinguishes representative tool roles. Analytical models evaluate encoded bounds; SCALE-Sim and Timeloop estimate accelerator cycles and traffic; gem5 models microarchitectural timing; Verilator runs RTL behavioral regression; FireSim executes mapped simulations on field-programmable gate array clusters; and physical EDA flows evaluate timing, power, and area under specified libraries and constraints. These observations can complement one another without forming a single ranking by accuracy.


A marked cell identifies a representative source of observations; it does not imply that all configurations of that tool answer the same question. For example, confirming a gem5-based ranking does not establish gate-level timing closure. The model's target, input representation, and reference path together define what its predictions mean. The next question is whether prediction error remains acceptable on the particular candidates the search selects.

## Predictor Support Boundaries {#sec-support-limits}

A predictor's measured accuracy applies to the candidates and conditions on which it was evaluated. Its qualified support is the range of designs, workloads, and implementation conditions for which that evaluation establishes useful performance. A new datapath structure or process corner may fall outside that range. Even within it, average root-mean-square error (RMSE) or mean absolute error can hide mistakes near the decision boundary. A model that usually estimates area well may still misclassify the candidates closest to the area limit.

Selection introduces another difficulty. An optimizer favors candidates with the best predicted values, so favorable prediction errors can influence which candidate wins. For the Lighthouse datapath, minimizing predicted energy can favor a design whose energy is underestimated. Maximizing predicted performance can favor an overestimate. This selection effect is the *optimizer's curse* [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. It can occur even when individual estimates are unbiased and the candidates remain within the evaluated region.

Missing architectural effects can compound that selection error. Consider a hypothetical out-of-order core study in which an instructions-per-cycle (IPC) proxy favors a 512-entry reorder buffer (ROB) paired with 16-wide issue. If the study assumes a fixed clock while omitting bypass-network and clock-distribution costs, the proposed core may fail timing at the target 3.0\ GHz. This is also a mismatch between the optimized proxy and the desired result: high simulated IPC alone does not establish performance at the required clock frequency. Confirmation must examine the property the study intends to improve.

Even individually unbiased estimates can become optimistic after selection. For fixed candidates with zero-mean estimation errors, $\hat{f}(x_i) = f(x_i) + \epsilon_i$, the expected maximum estimate is at least the maximum true value:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i=1,\dots,K} \hat{f}(x_i)\right] \ge \max_{i=1,\dots,K} f(x_i).
$${#eq-optimizers-curse-bias}

The maximum operation favors upward errors, which is why unbiased estimates do not imply an unbiased winning estimate (@eq-optimizers-curse-bias). The corresponding concern for minimization is a selected estimate that is too low. Preserve the predictions made before selection and reserve reference-tool confirmation runs so that the apparent gain can be compared with the confirmed gain. Refitting after a failed confirmation must not overwrite the prediction that led to the choice.

*Shrinkage* offers a further adjustment when a defensible error model is available. It pulls an extreme prediction toward a prior expectation, with greater adjustment when the estimate is less reliable [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. For an architecture surrogate, a practical empirical approach is to retain prediction-confirmation pairs from comparable searches and estimate how much of a predicted gain typically survives confirmation. The adjustment must be fitted separately from the candidates used to test it and checked under a comparable selection procedure. One failed finalist is insufficient to establish a reusable correction. Shrinkage moderates a prediction; it does not repair an omitted timing effect or replace the reference check.

::: {.callout-law title="The Optimizer's Curse in Proxy Search"}
**The Classical Principle:** Selecting the largest of individually unbiased estimates can make the selected estimate optimistic. The selection favors positive errors, even when the predictor has no average bias [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse].

**The Hardware Trap:** A search can favor an underestimated energy cost or an overestimated performance benefit. The core example adds an omitted physical constraint: optimizing IPC does not establish that the proposed organization meets its clock target.

**The Architectural Antidote:** Monitor uncertainty and screening error under the actual selection procedure, suspend screening when candidates leave declared support, and confirm finalists through reference checks matched to the claim. A physical timing claim requires timing evidence; a simulator-level ranking requires confirmation in its declared simulation conditions (@sec-law-optimizers-curse in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

The right accuracy measure depends on the predictor's job. For ranking, rank correlation ($r_s$) describes agreement over an ordering, while top-$k$ recall measures whether the predicted best set retains the measured best candidates.[^fn-ml-top-k-recall-c05] A good overall ranking can still miss the few candidates worth evaluating. For a hard power or timing limit, errors close to that threshold matter more directly. Qualification should therefore test the actual screening or selection rule, not only report average prediction error.

[^fn-ml-top-k-recall-c05]: **Top-k recall**: The fraction of the measured best $k$ candidates that also appear in the predictor's top $k$. Ansor uses top-k recall to ensure cost models retain promising tensor programs for subsequent evaluation [@ZhengEtAl2020Ansor].

Evaluate dedicated test batches from the intended candidate population through both the predictor and reference paths. If screening discards too many useful candidates, widen the survivor set, revise the rule, or suspend it while the cause is investigated. These checks consume part of the budget the surrogate aims to save. Changes in the candidate population can also weaken both predictions and uncertainty estimates [@OvadiaEtAl2019UncertaintyShift]. For a transition model, errors can accumulate as predicted states become inputs to later rollout steps.

A prediction interval provides another way to express uncertainty. If an area interval straddles the allowed limit, the estimate does not resolve feasibility and the candidate needs further evaluation. Split-conformal prediction[^fn-split-conformal-c05] constructs an interval using errors on a held-out calibration set [@LeiEtAl2018Conformal; @AngelopoulosBates2021Conformal]. First freeze the trained predictor $\hat{f}$. For each calibration candidate, compare its prediction with the reference observation $y_i$ and retain the absolute residual $|y_i-\hat{f}(x_i)|$. A high quantile of those residuals supplies a common error margin $q_{1-\alpha}$ around each new prediction:

$$
\hat{C}(x) = [\hat{f}(x) - q_{1-\alpha}, \, \hat{f}(x) + q_{1-\alpha}].
$$

For $n$ calibration examples, $q_{1-\alpha}$ is the $\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil$th smallest residual; if that rank exceeds $n$, the conservative margin is infinite. Here $1-\alpha$ is the desired coverage, and the rank correction accounts for the finite calibration sample. The guarantee requires *exchangeability*: the calibration examples and the next example must be statistically interchangeable, so their ordering carries no information about their joint distribution. Under that assumption, a new reference observation falls inside its interval with probability at least $1-\alpha$:

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(Y_{n+1} \in \hat{C}(X_{n+1})\right) \ge 1 - \alpha.
$$

Here, coverage means the probability that an interval contains the reference value. It differs from the screening coverage $f$ in @eq-screening-efficiency-bound, which measures the fraction of comparisons settled without a reference evaluation. A wide prediction interval can have high coverage while settling few design decisions.

The conformal guarantee is marginal: it applies to a new exchangeable sample, not separately to every design region or to whichever candidate an optimizer selects. Adaptive search can therefore invalidate the guarantee even before an obvious workload or process change. Once candidates no longer match the calibration conditions, the band width need not announce the failure. Tests for unfamiliar inputs can help identify changes, but cannot certify that the assumptions still hold.[^fn-ood-c05] Interval-based screening consequently needs reference checks on the candidate stream where it is used.

One monitoring rule compares the fraction of reference observations outside their predicted intervals over an audit window of $M$ cases with a declared tolerance: $\frac{1}{M}\sum_{k=1}^M \mathbb{I}(y_k \notin \hat{C}(x_k)) > \alpha + \epsilon_{\text{tol}}$. Here $\mathbb{I}$ is one when an observation falls outside its interval and zero otherwise. The window size and tolerance must account for sampling variation and repeated checks; crossing this threshold is an operational trigger, not by itself a statistical proof that coverage has changed. Audits must include candidates that screening would otherwise discard, since checking only survivors can miss harmful rejections. When the monitoring rule signals unreliable screening, two actions follow:

- **Suspend screening and escalate:** The system suspends surrogate screening and sends affected candidates to reference checks matched to the claimed property, at a rate the remaining evaluation capacity can support. A simulation ranking needs its declared simulator comparison; a physical timing claim needs a timing check.
- **Revise and requalify:** Retain the discrepant measurements for model revision, then qualify the revised predictor and its intervals on separate data from the intended candidate population before resuming screening. Retraining alone does not establish that the calibration assumptions hold again.

A calibrated interval is only as good as its support assumptions (@fig-ch05-conformal-coverage). The constructed example uses a nominal prediction-coverage target of 90%; its observed coverage inside the calibrated region ($x \le 6.0$) is about 96%. Beyond that region ($x > 6.0$), observed behavior leaves the fixed band and coverage collapses, which is what the coverage monitor is intended to detect.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-ch05-conformal-coverage
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **A calibrated interval depends on its support assumptions.** Constructed illustration of a
#|   split-conformal prediction band ($\pm q_{1-\alpha}$) around a latency-like surrogate curve. In the
#|   calibrated support regime on the left ($x \le 6.0$), observed prediction coverage is $\approx 96\%$
#|   for a nominal coverage target of 90%. When the workload regime shifts on the right ($x > 6.0$), the
#|   exchangeability assumption fails: observed values diverge from the surrogate, and empirical coverage
#|   collapses to $\approx 16\%$ despite the unchanged band width. A sustained coverage mismatch must halt
#|   predictor-based screening. All values are synthetic and illustrative.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of synthetic latency-like data with a fixed-width conformal prediction band around a surrogate curve. In the calibrated support region on the left, nearly all points fall inside the band; in the distribution-shift region on the right, observed behavior rises away from the unchanged band and most points escape it, showing coverage collapse."

import math
import random

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Constructed illustration: every value is synthetic, generated in this cell
# with a fixed seed; no real system was measured. The split-conformal recipe
# (calibration residual quantile -> fixed-width band) follows the conformal
# prediction pattern cited in the text.
rng = random.Random(20260713)
SHIFT_X = 6.0
NOISE = 0.32
X_MAX = 10.0

def surrogate(x):
    return 4.0 + 1.8 * math.sin(0.9 * x) + 0.25 * x

def truth(x):
    drift = 1.1 * (x - SHIFT_X) ** 1.25 if x > SHIFT_X else 0.0
    return surrogate(x) + drift

def observe(x):
    return truth(x) + rng.gauss(0.0, NOISE)

cal_x = [rng.uniform(0.0, SHIFT_X) for _ in range(60)]
cal_scores = sorted(abs(observe(x) - surrogate(x)) for x in cal_x)
q = cal_scores[math.ceil(0.9 * (len(cal_scores) + 1)) - 1]

test_in = [(x, observe(x)) for x in [0.15 + i * (SHIFT_X - 0.3) / 24 for i in range(25)]]
test_out = [(x, observe(x)) for x in [SHIFT_X + 0.15 + i * (X_MAX - SHIFT_X - 0.3) / 24 for i in range(25)]]
cov_in = sum(abs(y - surrogate(x)) <= q for x, y in test_in) / len(test_in)
cov_out = sum(abs(y - surrogate(x)) <= q for x, y in test_out) / len(test_out)

xs = [i * X_MAX / 400 for i in range(401)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.9, 2.55))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.11, right=0.97, top=0.86, bottom=0.19)

ax.fill_between(xs, [surrogate(x) - q for x in xs], [surrogate(x) + q for x in xs],
                color=COLORS["blue"], alpha=0.16, linewidth=0, zorder=1)
ax.plot(xs, [surrogate(x) for x in xs], color=COLORS["blue"], linewidth=1.1, zorder=2)
ax.plot(xs, [truth(x) for x in xs], color=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=0.9,
        linestyle=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=2)

ax.scatter([x for x, _ in test_in], [y for _, y in test_in], s=9,
           color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=3)
miss = [(x, y) for x, y in test_out if abs(y - surrogate(x)) > q]
hit = [(x, y) for x, y in test_out if abs(y - surrogate(x)) <= q]
ax.scatter([x for x, _ in hit], [y for _, y in hit], s=9, color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=3)
ax.scatter([x for x, _ in miss], [y for _, y in miss], s=11, color=COLORS["red"], zorder=3)

ax.axvline(SHIFT_X, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.7, linestyle="--", zorder=1)
ymin, ymax = ax.get_ylim()
ax.set_ylim(ymin, ymax + 1.2)
ax.text(SHIFT_X / 2, ax.get_ylim()[1] - 0.35, "calibrated support", ha="center",
        va="top", fontsize=6.0, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["workload_ink"])
ax.text((SHIFT_X + X_MAX) / 2, ax.get_ylim()[1] - 0.35, "changed workload regime",
        ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.0, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"])
ax.text(SHIFT_X / 2, ax.get_ylim()[1] - 1.15,
        f"empirical coverage ≈ {cov_in:.0%}\n(nominal 90%)", ha="center", va="top",
        fontsize=5.4, color=COLORS["workload_ink"])
ax.text((SHIFT_X + X_MAX) / 2, ax.get_ylim()[1] - 1.15,
        f"same band width,\ncoverage ≈ {cov_out:.0%}", ha="center", va="top",
        fontsize=5.4, color=COLORS["constraints_ink"])

ax.annotate("surrogate ± conformal band", (1.7, surrogate(1.7) + q),
            textcoords="offset points", xytext=(-2, 5), fontsize=5.6,
            color=COLORS["workload_ink"])
ax.annotate("observed behavior", (8.2, truth(8.2)), textcoords="offset points",
            xytext=(-58, 2), fontsize=5.6, color=COLORS["muted"])

ax.set_xlabel("workload / design parameter (synthetic units)", fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylabel("latency-like metric\n(synthetic units)", fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlim(0, X_MAX)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6.5, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6)
for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The fixed band in the illustration does not widen when the observations move away from it. Detecting that mismatch requires new reference observations, and qualifying a revised screening rule requires separate checks (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). Prediction is useful only while it preserves the distinctions needed for the decision. It also presumes that candidate artifacts exist to be evaluated; constructing or revising those artifacts is the next method's job.

## Synthesizing Candidate Architecture Artifacts

Generation produces the artifact that a predictor or evaluator will examine. For the illustrative Lighthouse datapath, the starting information includes the required computation, numerical behavior, interface, and implementation constraints. A generator may construct an initial RTL implementation or revise an existing one after feedback exposes a limitation. Its output needs enough structure to enter the tool flow: a proposed organization expressed as code or another executable design representation.

Suppose implementation feedback identifies a long arithmetic path. A generator could propose a different arrangement of operations or an additional pipeline boundary, if the interface permits the latency change. The revised artifact would then undergo functional and implementation checks. If the added registers increase area or switching activity too much, the next revision could pursue a different organization. Arithmetic rewrites must preserve the specified behavior, including rounding and overflow where relevant. The feedback thus guides structural revision, rather than merely assigning a score to an unchanged candidate set.

Different construction techniques make different changes easy to express. A parameterized template fills in choices within a supplied structure. Compiler transformations rewrite an existing representation using available rules; Halide illustrates how computation and scheduling choices can be separated [@RaganKelleyEtAl2017HalideCACM]. A grammar constructs artifacts from permitted productions, while a solver searches for assignments satisfying encoded constraints. These approaches can preserve known structure and provide strong conventional alternatives to learned generation.

An autoregressive code model constructs a sequence by predicting successive tokens from the supplied context and the tokens already produced [@Chen2021Codex; @ThakurEtAl2023VeriGen]. Although its mechanism is token prediction, its engineering output is a candidate program, so it performs generation in this chapter's terminology. A graph generator instead constructs represented nodes and connections. For spatial artifacts, diffusion models generate placements through iterative denoising; guided sampling can steer the result toward placement objectives [@LeeEtAl2025DiffusionPlacement]. The representation and construction mechanism jointly determine which alternatives are reachable.

Project information can enter a learned generator in different ways. Retrieval supplies relevant specifications or examples at generation time. Fine-tuning changes model parameters using training examples. ChipNeMo investigates domain adaptation and retrieval for chip-design tasks [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]; neither mechanism guarantees that a generated artifact obeys the current specification. The permitted use of training and retrieved material, and restrictions on sending proprietary RTL or foundry process design kit (PDK) information to external services, remain part of the data requirements in @sec-architecture-data-access. @tbl-generation-techniques connects these construction paths to the artifacts they produce and the checks those artifacts still need.

| **Artifact or problem** | **Likely construction path** | **What the path can enforce or use** | **External check still required** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structured configuration / program | Template, grammar generator, solver, program synthesis. | Encoded syntax, types, and constraints. | Intended semantics and runtime behavior. |
| Software, script, or compiler code | Autoregressive model, LLM, constrained decoding. | Supplied context and schema restrictions. | Execution semantics and target behavior. |
| RTL | Autoregressive model / LLM evaluated with hardware benchmarks [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM]. | Supplied design context and grammar constraints. | Elaboration, clock-domain crossing (CDC) linting, reset sync, simulation, SVA/BMC formal checks, synthesis in Yosys, STA in OpenSTA, power analysis under UPF intent, and physical signoff for implementation claims. |
| Project-specific text or code | Retrieval-supported generation. | Retrieved documents and examples. | Source consistency and artifact-specific checks. |
| Netlist / connectivity object | Graph-generative / conditioned model. | Represented nodes, edges, graph constraints. | Electrical, functional, timing, and physical checks. |
| Placement or floorplan | Diffusion or spatial generator [@LeeEtAl2025DiffusionPlacement]. | Spatial distributions and boundary geometry. | Legalization, routing, timing, power, and design rule checking (DRC). |
| Mixed hard and learned constraints | Learned proposal plus solver, compiler, or repair step. | Hard constraints from solver; patterns from data. | Properties not established by encoded constraints. |
: **Generative techniques should match artifacts and available constraints.** Enforcing syntax during construction prunes invalid drafts but does not replace property-specific verification. {#tbl-generation-techniques tbl-colwidths="[22,26,28,24]"}

The table separates constraints enforced during construction from properties established afterward. Constrained decoding restricts output to the enforced grammar [@WillardLouf2023GuidedGeneration; @GengEtAl2023GrammarConstrained]. Syntactically valid SystemVerilog can still contain unintended latches, conflicting drivers, missing reset logic, or clock-domain crossing errors. VerilogEval and RTLLM examine generated RTL through benchmark-specific checks [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM]; success on those checks does not establish complete physical signoff. The RTL row therefore includes bounded model checking (BMC)[^fn-bmc-c05] for encoded behavioral properties and static timing analysis (STA)[^fn-sta-c05] for constrained circuit paths.

Combining learned proposals with symbolic checks can eliminate some defects early. Abstract syntax tree (AST) checks and static compiler passes examine program structure; Boolean satisfiability (SAT) and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers can check encoded constraints. The constraints also delimit the alternatives construction can explore. A grammar that fixes the pipeline structure cannot generate a new pipeline organization, even if it produces many textually different implementations. Candidate diversity therefore needs to be judged in terms of hardware structure and behavior, not only different source strings.

Generated tests need the same scrutiny as generated designs. If both repeat a specification misunderstanding, agreement between them can hide the defect. Reference behavior, independently derived properties, or another suitable checking path must be capable of exposing that shared error.

Resource constraints matter during construction as well. In a high-level synthesis (HLS) pragma search, aggressive loop unrolling can exhaust field-programmable gate array (FPGA) block RAM or create routing congestion even when the generated code is legal. The constructor needs physical resource bounds, and the resulting artifact still needs implementation checks.

KernelBench[^fn-kernelbench-c05] makes the distinction between producing an artifact, passing its tests, and improving performance concrete. It evaluates generated CUDA kernels against PyTorch baselines [@OuyangEtAl2025KernelBench]. The correctness and speed results in @fig-ch05-kernel-funnel show why counting generated candidates alone gives little indication of useful output.

